headline: NZ Fuel Relief Expands as Parliament Votes to End Greyhound Racing
summary: Parliament debated the effects of Middle East conflict on fuel prices, with the Government outlining new diesel storage and targeted payments while resisting calls for broader public transport subsidies or a general work-from-home push. MPs also approved the closure of commercial greyhound racing and advanced contentious bills on retail trespass and alcohol licensing. The House adjourned until 21 April.

topicSummaries.topic: Fuel Response Adds Diesel Storage and Targeted Household Support
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Higher fuel prices are squeezing household budgets and businesses, while the Government’s measures affect support payments and the country’s ability to manage a possible supply disruption.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis said fuel was continuing to flow, with no immediate supply disruption, but that global prices were putting pressure on households and businesses. The Government approved a proposal to add up to 93 million litres of diesel storage at Marsden Point, about a 20 percent increase in current capacity, and is examining options to secure extra supply. It also plans to increase the in-work tax credit by $50 a week for about 143,000 families, with a smaller abated payment for another 14,000. Health Minister Simeon Brown announced a 30 percent temporary increase in mileage rates for home and community support workers, as well as for eligible patients travelling for treatment. Ministers said further fuel-response phases were not yet needed; Opposition MPs questioned how essential services would operate if shortages worsened.

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Brewer (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What further actions is the Government considering to bolster fuel supply?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Yesterday, Ministers signed off on a proposal through the Regional Infrastructure Fund to increase New Zealand’s diesel storage capacity through a commercial arrangement with Channel Infrastructure at Marsden Point. This will provide up to an additional 93 million litres of diesel storage, which is around a 20 percent increase in current capacity

topicSummaries.topic: Government and Greens Clash Over Public Transport Funding
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns whether people facing high fuel costs will have more frequent or cheaper alternatives to driving, particularly in regional towns.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Julie Anne Genter urged the Government to fund more frequent bus services and reconsider cuts to public transport concessions and vehicle electrification. Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the Government was monitoring capacity but prioritising existing services because land-transport revenue was forecast to fall while diesel costs were rising. He said further investment could be considered if capacity pressures emerged, but rejected new services and broad subsidies as immediate priorities. Genter also argued that investing in more frequent services could increase demand and help people switch from cars.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that demand for public transport is influenced by the supply, and that if a bus is coming every 15 minutes in smaller towns like Dunedin, New Plymouth, Whanganui, Levin, there will be more demand for public transport, and what will he do to provide services?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our focus is on maintaining existing services so that they can continue to operate, because the last thing I would want to see at this time of great peril is people not being able to take public transport when they need to make the switch out of their cars.

topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law ends commercial greyhound racing in New Zealand from 1 August 2026 and sets up a transition process for affected workers and an estimated 1,600 dogs needing homes.
topicSummaries.content: Parliament passed the Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Bill at its third and final reading, with National, Labour, the Greens, New Zealand First, Te Pāti Māori and independent MP Tākuta Ferris voting in favour; ACT voted against. Supporters cited repeated reviews, injuries and deaths, and argued that further reforms would not adequately improve animal welfare. The bill establishes a transition agency to oversee the closure, support affected people, and coordinate care and rehoming. The agency is expected to provide retraining and wellbeing support, but amendments for direct compensation were not adopted. TAB betting on overseas greyhound races will continue under the bill, with a review required later. ACT’s Cameron Luxton opposed the closure, arguing that industry participants deserved greater involvement and compensation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Casey Costello (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: At the heart of this bill and all the decision making that has led us to this point are, first and foremost, greyhounds and the people.

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Luxton (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Compensation sets the right precedent. It says that Parliament respects property rights.

topicSummaries.topic: Retail Trespass Bill Advances Despite Rights and Access Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could let retailers exclude people from multiple stores, including supermarket chains, affecting both worker safety and some people’s access to essential shopping.
topicSummaries.content: The House gave the Trespass (Specified Retail Premises and Other Matters) Amendment Bill its first reading and referred it to the Justice Committee, with a report due by 3 August. The bill would extend trespass notices from two years to three, allow notices to cover multiple retail, hospitality or licensed premises, and increase some penalties. Ministers and ACT argued the measures would help protect retailers and staff from repeat offending. Labour supported sending the bill to select committee but raised questions about privacy, children’s rights and provisions under which someone might be deemed to know they had been trespassed. The Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the bill, warning about freedom of movement, potential disproportionate effects on Māori and Pasifika, and the risk of excluding people from essential services.

keyExchanges.speaker: Parmjeet Parmar (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: if you threaten people’s safety and if you threaten people’s livelihood, there will be consequences; and yes, your privilege of access to their business can be taken away.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rawiri Waititi (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Giving businesses the power to ban people from entering stores they’ve never been to—for any reason—is not justice.

topicSummaries.topic: Alcohol Licensing Reforms Pass First Reading Amid Harm Debate
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would narrow who can object to alcohol licences and change rules for clubs, venues and retailers, potentially affecting both local participation and alcohol availability.
topicSummaries.content: The Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Improving Alcohol Regulation) Amendment Bill passed its first reading by 68 votes to 55 and was referred to the Justice Committee. Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee said it would reduce compliance costs and modernise licensing, including by generally limiting objections to people who live or work in the same council area or within one kilometre of a proposed premises. The bill would also expand licensing options for clubs and some hospitality businesses, and clarify responsibilities for alcohol delivery services. Labour and Green MPs argued that restricting objections could weaken community influence and alcohol-harm protections; they also raised concerns about the placement of zero-alcohol drinks. Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Ferris voted against the first reading.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicole McKee (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: The process simply reflects who is actually affected

keyExchanges.speaker: Georgie Dansey (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The main issue with this bill is that reducing regulation and reducing community voice in decision making causes more alcohol harm in our community.

topicSummaries.topic: Minister Defends Plan to Disestablish Environment Ministry
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed restructuring has raised questions about whether environmental advice and oversight will remain effective, including for regions facing repeated severe weather.
topicSummaries.content: Green MPs challenged Environment Minister Penny Simmonds over the Government’s decision to disestablish the Ministry for the Environment. Simmonds said the changes were structural and technical, with no substantive change to the ministry’s statutory functions or environmental protections, and argued that bringing related portfolios together could improve coordination. Critics cited concerns from submitters and environmental advocates about the effect on environmental outcomes and the loss of a dedicated voice for the environment at the centre of government. Asked about safeguards for vulnerable regions, Simmonds said statutory reporting and advice to ministers would continue; no new specific safeguards were outlined in the exchange.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lan Pham (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Will the Government’s decision to disestablish the Ministry for the Environment result in better or worse environmental outcomes?

keyExchanges.speaker: Penny Simmonds (National)
keyExchanges.quote: There are no substantive changes to the functions under the Environment Act 1986. There is no reduction in environmental protections. The amendments are structural and technical only.

topicSummaries.topic: Regional Vocational Training Gets New Structures and Funding
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The announced changes and investments are intended to maintain local training options and support education linked to regional jobs and industries.
topicSummaries.content: Vocational Education Minister Penny Simmonds outlined new arrangements due to begin in 2027, with NorthTec, the Western Institute of Technology at Taranaki, Whitireia and WelTec becoming stand-alone regional polytechnics supported by a federation. Tai Poutini Polytechnic will operate within the Open Polytechnic, with the Government saying campus-based provision on the West Coast would continue. Simmonds also announced an in-principle $34.7 million for a Whangārei tertiary hub, subject to a business case, $10 million for rebuilding and improving the Eastern Institute of Technology’s Taradale campus after Cyclone Gabrielle, and $2.4 million for maintenance at Telford’s agricultural training campus.

keyExchanges.speaker: Grant McCallum (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What does this announcement mean for Northland?

keyExchanges.speaker: Penny Simmonds (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I am delighted to announce the in-principle investment of $34.7 million for the development of a new Whangārei tertiary hub—subject to business case

conclusion: The sitting ended with a clear legislative win for the greyhound racing closure, while disputes over fuel costs, public services, retail powers and alcohol regulation remain unresolved.
